searchText: Nah I did it all wrong lol. Nishant was already doing it so I just closed my PR has anyone studied whether the attestations that get put into blocks actually are useful / make sense? ie every block right now has 128 attestations basically which slows down block processing and thus the network in general, but is it the case that all of those attestations cause some profit? there are certainly entirely redundant attestations in there I've checked just through manual inspection and regularly find strict subsets of other attestations in the same block but haven't do an analysis well, they could still be profitable > slows down block processing and thus the network in general That said, if 128 can't be handled efficiently (I'm pretty sure it can be), then that would be grounds for tuning constants well, it's 128 validations + 128*N public key aggregations _strict subsets_ meaning one attestation has validators [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] for vote A and another has validators [2, 3] also for vote A that second attestation would not be profitable in the same block right, missed s trict if you included the second attestaion in block N and the 1st in block N+1 then it would be profitable > well, it's 128 validations + 128*N public key aggregations yes, understood, so it will take longer, but if these large blocks "slow down the network" then we have a deeper problem with configuration choices sure - it's more that it eats into the security margin that we have, but there's no _direct_ economic incentive to not includde them self preservation 🙂 but agreed, if it were computationally hard to figure out a good packing, then it might be rational to just pack whatever and full not sure if it can be turned into an attack as well - I mean, it's actually interesting to see what the maximum number of operations is per block and then benchmark the libraries against that

excerpts.content: Nah I did it all wrong lol. Nishant was already doing it so I just closed my PR

excerpts.author: arnetheduck
excerpts.content: has anyone studied whether the attestations that get put into blocks actually are useful / make sense? ie every block right now has 128 attestations basically which slows down block processing and thus the network in general, but is it the case that all of those attestations cause some profit?

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: there are certainly entirely redundant attestations in there

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: I've checked just through manual inspection and regularly find strict subsets of other attestations in the same block

excerpts.author: arnetheduck
excerpts.content: well, they could still be profitable

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
> slows down block processing and thus the network in general
That said, if 128 can't be handled efficiently (I'm pretty sure it can be), then that would be grounds for tuning constants

excerpts.author: arnetheduck
excerpts.content: well, it's 128 validations + 128*N public key aggregations

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
_strict subsets_

meaning one attestation has validators [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] for vote A and another has validators [2, 3] also for vote A

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: that second attestation would not be profitable in the same block

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: if you included the second attestaion in block N and the 1st in block N+1 then it would be profitable

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content:
> well, it's 128 validations + 128*N public key aggregations
yes, understood, so it will take longer, but if these large blocks "slow down the network" then we have a deeper problem with configuration choices

excerpts.author: arnetheduck
excerpts.content: sure - it's more that it eats into the security margin that we have, but there's no _direct_ economic incentive to not includde them

excerpts.author: djrtwo
excerpts.content: but agreed, if it were computationally hard to figure out a good packing, then it might be rational to just pack whatever and full
